<ConflictType>Conflicting opinions and research outcomes</ConflictType> — Retrieved studies present opposing conclusions on whether antidepressants outperform placebo.

The evidence clusters into two contradictory positions: d1, d3, d4, d5, and d6 report a large meta-analysis finding all 21 antidepressants more effective than placebo. In contrast, d2, d7, d8, d9, and d10 argue the drug-placebo difference is minimal or relevant only for a minority, suggesting antidepressants are not meaningfully more effective for most people. This represents a fundamental disagreement on research outcomes within the scientific literature.

Given the conflicting opinions, a definitive yes/no answer cannot be provided. The retrieved set itself contains the controversy, with high-quality sources on both sides (e.g., Lancet vs. BMJ/FDA analyses). The final answer must neutrally present these opposing viewpoints as reflected in the research.

The question of whether antidepressants are more effective than placebo is subject to ongoing scientific debate with conflicting research outcomes. A major 2018 meta-analysis of 522 trials concluded all 21 antidepressants studied were more effective than placebo at reducing symptoms [d1, d4, d6]. However, other analyses, including an FDA participant-level study, found the average drug-placebo difference is minimal and that the observed advantage likely affects only a minority of patients [d2, d8]. Some researchers argue that much of the observed improvement is a placebo response, questioning the drugs' specific efficacy [d7, d9]. This reflects a persistent conflict in the scientific literature over interpreting the clinical significance of antidepressant effects.
